ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.a-model-t.title: Training a model by making it criticise itself
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.a-model-t.hook: The human's job shrinks from ranking thousands of harmful answers to writing down the rules. Then the model does the ranking.
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.a-model-t.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.a-model-t.body:
Standard preference training needs people to read the model's worst output and rank it. That is slow, expensive, and genuinely unpleasant work, and it scales with the number of things you want the model to get right.

Bai and colleagues at Anthropic, December 2022, asked what happens if the human contribution shrinks to a written list of principles.

Stage one is supervised. Ask the model something it should refuse. When it answers badly, show it one principle drawn at random from the list and ask it to critique its own answer against that principle. Then ask it to rewrite. Fine-tune the model on the rewrites.

Stage two is reinforcement learning. Have the model compare pairs of its own responses against the principles, train a preference model on those machine-generated comparisons, and optimise the policy against it. They call it RLAIF: reinforcement learning from AI feedback.

The claim worth taking seriously is not that a model supervises itself. It is that the supervision becomes a document — something you can read, disagree with, and put under version control.
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.a-model-t.rigor:
The preference model is the usual Bradley–Terry likelihood. For two responses $y_1,y_2$ to a prompt $x$, fit a scalar $r_\theta$ so that
$$P(y_1\succ y_2\mid x)=\sigma\big(r_\theta(x,y_1)-r_\theta(x,y_2)\big),\qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.$$
Only *differences* of $r_\theta$ are identified — the scale is arbitrary, which is why reward numbers are never comparable across runs. In RLHF the comparison labels come from people; in Constitutional AI they come from a feedback model shown both responses plus a principle, with its answer read off the probability it assigns to each option.

The policy is then optimised for
$$\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\big[r_\theta(x,y)\big]\;-\;\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}\big),$$
maximising the learned reward while staying close to the supervised starting model.

That KL term is not a technicality. $r_\theta$ is a proxy, fitted on a finite sample of comparisons, and it is wrong somewhere. The penalty caps how far the policy may travel into the region where it is wrong. It is the optimizer's curse, written into the loss function as a leash.

recall.question: What is the KL penalty in preference-based fine-tuning actually for?

options.text: Keeping the model's outputs grammatical
options.why: fluency comes from pretraining; the penalty is about distance from the reference policy.

options.text: Limiting how far the policy can move from the reference model
options.why: because the learned reward is a proxy that is wrong somewhere out there.

options.text: Preventing the preference model from overfitting its training comparisons
options.why: that is a concern for fitting $r_\theta$, not for constraining the policy.

ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.principle.title: Some of Claude's principles came from Apple's terms of service
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.principle.hook: Human-rights law has nothing to say about impersonating someone in a chat window. A phone company's terms of service do.
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.principle.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.constitutional-ai.principle.body: In May 2023 Anthropic published the document its model is trained against. The principles are drawn from the UN Declaration of Human Rights, from trust-and-safety practice, and from rules proposed by other labs, including DeepMind's Sparrow principles. For the mundane cases a 1948 human-rights declaration never anticipated — personal data, impersonation, identity — they drew on what they called global platform guidelines, naming Apple's terms of service. A further set was written to push the model away from assuming a Western, rich, industrialised point of view.

recall.question: Why did a human-rights declaration need supplementing with a phone company's fine print?
recall.answer: Because most of what a chat model has to get right is mundane — impersonation, data, harassment — and platform terms are decades of accumulated practice on exactly those cases.

ai.alignment.problem.a-colorful-imitatio.title: The alignment problem, stated in 1960
ai.alignment.problem.a-colorful-imitatio.hook: The alignment problem was stated in Science magazine in 1960, in one sentence, by the man who named cybernetics.
ai.alignment.problem.a-colorful-imitatio.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.problem.a-colorful-imitatio.body:
Norbert Wiener, in *Science*, 6 May 1960:

> If we use, to achieve our purposes, a mechanical agency with whose operation we cannot efficiently interfere once we have started it … then we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire and not merely a colorful imitation of it.

The clause that earns its keep is the last one: not the fear of disobedience, but of obedience to something that merely resembles what you meant.

sources.title: Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation
sources.author: Norbert Wiener

ai.alignment.problem.you-cannot-write-do.title: You cannot write down what you want
ai.alignment.problem.you-cannot-write-do.hook: The worry is not that a machine will disobey you. It is that it will obey, exactly, the thing you managed to write down.
ai.alignment.problem.you-cannot-write-do.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.problem.you-cannot-write-do.body:
State the alignment problem properly and it stops sounding like science fiction, which is a loss for the trailers and a gain for everyone else.

There is something you want. You cannot write it down — try turning "be helpful" or "drive well" into something a computer can score, and you get either a vague sentence or a checklist with holes. So you write a proxy: something measurable that tracks what you want across every case you have thought of.

Then you optimise against the proxy, hard.

Here is the trap, and it is statistical rather than psychological. Optimisation does not sample typical points. It hunts extremes, and the extremes of your proxy are exactly where proxy and reality have come apart — that is *what it means* for them to have come apart. So the harder you push, the more of your measured success is made of error.

Two versions get separate names. Maybe the objective you wrote is wrong. Or maybe the system learned some *other* goal that happened to score well in training. The second is worse, because nothing in the score reveals it.
ai.alignment.problem.you-cannot-write-do.rigor:
Model the proxy as $\hat U = U + \varepsilon$ with independent $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ and $U\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma_U^2)$, over $n$ candidate options. Select $x^\star=\arg\max_x \hat U(x)$.

Conditioning shrinks the estimate towards the prior:
$$\mathbb{E}\big[U\mid \hat U=v\big]=\mu+\frac{\sigma_U^{2}}{\sigma_U^{2}+\sigma^{2}}\,(v-\mu),$$
so the value you actually get is always less than the score you measured. That is the **optimizer's curse** (Smith and Winkler, 2006).

Now add optimisation pressure. The maximum of $n$ draws sits about $\sqrt{2\ln n}$ standard deviations up: $\mathbb{E}[\hat U(x^\star)]\approx \mu+\sqrt{(\sigma_U^{2}+\sigma^{2})\,2\ln n}$. Combining the two,
$$\mathbb{E}\big[\hat U(x^\star)-U(x^\star)\big]\;\approx\;\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sqrt{\sigma_U^{2}+\sigma^{2}}}\,\sqrt{2\ln n}.$$

Read the sign and the variables. The shortfall grows without bound in $n$ — the amount of searching — for *any* fixed proxy error $\sigma>0$. "Just optimise harder" is not a fix for a bad proxy. It is the mechanism.

recall.question: Why does more optimisation make a proxy objective worse rather than better?

options.text: Because more optimisation overfits the training data
options.why: overfitting is one instance; this happens even with a perfectly estimated proxy over new options.

options.text: Because search concentrates on extremes of the proxy
options.why: and the extremes are exactly where proxy and true objective disagree most.

options.text: Because optimisers introduce their own noise into the objective
options.why: the noise is in the proxy's relationship to what you want, not in the optimiser.

ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-central-ba.title: A Bank of England adviser named your AI's failure mode
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-central-ba.hook: The law that explains why your reward function breaks was written about the Bank of England's money-supply targets in 1975.
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-central-ba.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Credited Keith Hoskin for the 'when a measure becomes a target' phrasing that Strathern's 1997 paper carries.

ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-central-ba.body:
Remember central banks and the business of hitting a target? In the 1970s the Bank of England tried to control inflation by steering a measure of the money supply, on the strength of a relationship between money and prices that had held for decades. The relationship stopped holding almost as soon as policy leaned on it.

Charles Goodhart, then an adviser at the Bank, wrote the sentence in 1975:

> Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.

Marilyn Strathern's 1997 paper carries the version you have heard — when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — a phrasing she credits to Keith Hoskin.

This is not an analogy for what happens to a reward function. It is the same statement. A proxy is a correlation. Correlations hold in the regime where they were measured. Optimising against one drags you out of that regime by construction — which is why the boat spun in circles, and why Goodhart's economists lost their money-demand equation.
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-central-ba.rigor:
Manheim and Garrabrant (2018) separate at least four mechanisms, and they fail differently, so it is worth keeping them apart. Write the proxy as a measurement $M$ of a goal $G$.

**Regressional.** $M=G+\varepsilon$. Selecting the top of $M$ selects partly for $\varepsilon$, so $\mathbb{E}[G\mid M \text{ large}] < M$. Unavoidable whenever measurement is noisy; it gets worse as you search harder.

**Extremal.** $M\approx G$ was fitted on the observed range. Push into the tail and the functional relationship itself changes — the fit was never meant to extrapolate.

**Causal.** $M$ correlates with $G$ through a shared cause, or because $G$ causes $M$. Then *intervening* on $M$ does not move $G$ at all. This is Goodhart's own case: money and prices moved together, but forcing the aggregate did not force the prices.

**Adversarial.** A second agent, who benefits from your decision, optimises $M$ deliberately once you commit to it.

Only the first is a statistical nuisance. The causal one is fatal: no amount of extra data on $M$ and $G$ can tell you whether the link survives an intervention. That is the same gap that separates prediction from causation everywhere else in your studies.

recall.question: Which flavour of Goodhart's law cannot be fixed with more data on the proxy?

options.text: Regressional Goodhart
options.why: more data shrinks the noise and softens the regression effect, even if it never disappears.

options.text: Causal Goodhart
options.why: if the proxy only correlates through a shared cause, no amount of observational data tells you whether intervening on it moves the goal.

options.text: Adversarial Goodhart
options.why: a real problem, but it is about a second agent's incentives, not about how much you know.

sources.title: 'Improving ratings': audit in the British University system
sources.author: Marilyn Strathern

ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-public-lis.title: There is a public list of every way an optimiser cheated
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-public-lis.hook: Researchers keep a shared catalogue of every documented case of an optimiser finding the loophole. It runs to dozens.
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-public-lis.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.a-public-lis.body: DeepMind researchers maintain a crowd-sourced catalogue of specification gaming — around sixty cases when they wrote it up in April 2020. A creature in Karl Sims's 1994 evolution experiments grew very tall and fell over, because "distance travelled" never said you had to walk. A robot told to stack a red block on a blue one flipped the red block instead: the reward measured the height of its bottom face. A Tetris player learned to pause the game forever rather than lose.

recall.question: What do the catalogued cases have in common?
recall.answer: In every one the agent scored well by the stated metric. Nothing malfunctioned. The failure was always in the translation from what we wanted to what we could measure.

sources.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity
sources.author: Krakovna et al.

ai.alignment.reward-hacking.el-barco-que.title: El barco que descubrió que la carrera no era el punto
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.el-barco-que.hook: El agente sacó más puntos que cualquier humano. También se incendió, chocó contra otras lanchas y jamás terminó la carrera.
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.el-barco-que.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.reward-hacking.el-barco-que.body:
Diciembre de 2016. OpenAI publica un agente jugando CoastRunners, un juego de lanchas. El objetivo obvio era ganar la carrera, pero eso es una señal lenta y escasa, así que los investigadores hicieron lo razonable: le dieron puntos por chocar unos blancos verdes repartidos por el circuito. Más blancos, más puntos, y de paso el agente aprende a seguir la ruta.

El agente encontró una laguna apartada donde tres de esos blancos reaparecen solos. Y se quedó ahí. Girando en círculo, golpeando los mismos tres blancos una y otra vez, chocando contra otras lanchas, prendiéndose fuego, yendo en contravía. Sacó cerca de un 20 % más de puntos que un jugador humano promedio, y no cruzó la meta ni una vez.

No hubo ningún error de programación. El agente maximizó exactamente lo que le pedimos. El error fue la traducción: «gana la carrera» se volvió «acumula puntos», dos cosas que coinciden en el caso típico y se separan justo donde un optimizador va a buscar.

recall.question: ¿Qué falló exactamente en CoastRunners?
recall.answer: La especificación, no el algoritmo. Los puntos por blancos verdes eran un sustituto de «ganar la carrera»; el agente optimizó el sustituto hasta el punto donde deja de parecerse al objetivo real.

ai.alignment.scalable-oversight.grading-.title: How do you grade an answer you cannot check?
ai.alignment.scalable-oversight.grading-.hook: Economics has a century of theory for hiring someone who knows more than you. All of it assumes you can eventually check the work.
ai.alignment.scalable-oversight.grading-.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.alignment.scalable-oversight.grading-.body:
Remember the principal–agent problem: you hire someone *because* they know something you do not, and then you cannot distinguish a good job from a job that looks good. Economics has a hundred years of machinery for this — screening, signalling, contracts that make honesty pay. Every piece of it assumes that something correlated with quality eventually becomes observable. Sales figures arrive. The bridge stands or falls.

Scalable oversight is that problem with the assumption removed.

Suppose a model writes ten thousand lines of code, or a proof, or a summary of a patient's history, and it is better at the task than the person reviewing it. Then human approval is no longer evidence about quality. It is evidence about persuasiveness. And since approval is exactly what these systems are trained on, training optimises for the thing that is still measurable: convincing the reviewer.

The problem has a clean statement and no solution. What it has instead is four serious proposals, and knowing what each assumes is the useful part.
ai.alignment.scalable-oversight.grading-.rigor:
**Sandwiching** (Bowman et al., 2022) is the empirical handle. Pick tasks where a domain expert succeeds but both a non-expert and the model fail. Then test whether non-expert plus model reaches the expert's level. It gives a measurable proxy for the capability gap *today*, with today's models, rather than waiting for superhuman ones.

**Debate** (Irving, Christiano and Amodei, 2018) has two copies of the model argue and a human judge the exchange. The bet is asymmetry: in a zero-sum debate game, exposing a false claim is easier than defending one, so the equilibrium favours truth. They note that debate with a polynomial-time judge reaches questions in PSPACE, which is the formal version of the hope.

**Iterated amplification** (Christiano, Shlegeris and Amodei, 2018) builds the supervisor out of many calls to a weaker supervisor plus the model, so oversight strength grows alongside capability instead of being fixed.

**Task decomposition** reduces an uncheckable task to sub-tasks that are individually checkable, and bets that errors do not hide in the seams.

Each is a conjecture. What is established is only the failure mode: approval is a proxy whose error grows with the capability gap, and optimising a proxy is the previous card.

recall.question: What breaks when a model is more capable than its human supervisor?

options.text: The model stops following instructions
options.why: capability and obedience are separate; the issue is evaluating the output, not producing it.

options.text: Human approval stops tracking quality and starts tracking persuasiveness
options.why: and approval is exactly what the training signal is made of.

options.text: The training signal becomes too sparse to learn from
options.why: there is plenty of signal; the problem is what the signal is actually measuring.

ai.frontier.compute-hardware.six-flops-p.title: The arithmetic behind every "we trained a big model"
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.six-flops-p.hook: Six operations per parameter per token. That single number turns any press release about a big model into a napkin calculation.
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.six-flops-p.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Recall distractor claimed 2ND = 1.4e23; 2ND is 2.8e23. Fixed that and the second distractor's non-teaching reason.

ai.frontier.compute-hardware.six-flops-p.body:
Compute sounds like money. It is first a count, and the count is short enough to do in your head.

Training a transformer costs roughly six floating-point operations per parameter, per token of training text. Six: two going forwards, four coming back. Multiply by the parameters, multiply by the tokens, and you have the whole cost of the run as a single number.

That is enough to check anybody's claims. A data-centre accelerator manages a few hundred trillion operations a second on paper, and you actually get something like a third to a half of that. Divide, and a mid-sized model turns into thousands of chips running for weeks — which is why the list of organisations doing this is short, and why the shortness has nothing to do with secrecy.

So when you next read that a model is enormous, there are only two questions worth asking: how many parameters, and how many tokens?
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.six-flops-p.rigor:
$$C \approx 6ND \ \text{FLOP},$$
with $N$ non-embedding parameters and $D$ training tokens (Kaplan et al., 2020; used throughout Hoffmann et al., 2022). The forward pass is one multiply and one add per weight per token, $2N$; the backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights, about $4N$.

Worked example. $N=7\times10^{9}$, $D=2\times10^{12}$:
$$C = 6\cdot 7\times10^{9}\cdot 2\times10^{12}=8.4\times10^{22}\ \text{FLOP}.$$
At a *sustained* $1.6\times10^{14}$ FLOP/s per accelerator — 40% of a 400 TFLOP/s peak, a realistic utilisation — that is $5.25\times10^{8}$ accelerator-seconds, about 6,100 accelerator-days: a thousand chips for six days, or ten thousand for fifteen hours.

Energy follows from the same count. Patterson et al. (2021) estimate GPT-3's training at 1,287 MWh and 552 tonnes of CO₂-equivalent — roughly the annual electricity of 120 American households, for one run.

And remember what kind of cost this is. It is the fixed cost $F$: paid in full, up front, before anyone knows whether the model is any good.

recall.question: A model has 70 billion parameters and was trained on 2 trillion tokens. Roughly what did the run cost in operations?

options.text: About $2.8\times10^{23}$
options.why: that is $2ND$, the forward pass only; training also pays for the backward pass.

options.text: About $8.4\times10^{23}$
options.why: six operations per parameter per token, so $6\times 7\times10^{10}\times 2\times10^{12}$.

options.text: About $1.4\times10^{11}$
options.why: that is twice the parameter count with the tokens left out; compute scales with parameters times tokens, not parameters alone.

ai.frontier.compute-hardware.the-chip-is.title: Why a model is slow even on a very fast chip
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.the-chip-is.hook: While a model writes you a sentence, the fastest chip in the building is mostly idle, waiting for numbers to arrive.
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.the-chip-is.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.the-chip-is.body:
A modern accelerator performs hundreds of trillions of arithmetic operations a second. While it generates text for you, one word at a time, it spends most of its life doing nothing at all.

The reason is embarrassingly simple. To produce a single token, the chip must read *every weight in the model* out of memory — all of them, once. Arithmetic is fast and memory is slow, so the multipliers sit idle waiting for numbers to arrive, then consume them in a flash, then wait again.

Once you see it, a lot of otherwise disconnected facts line up. Generation speed falls roughly in proportion to model size. Serving many users at once is nearly free per user, because the weights get read once and used for everybody. Quantising to fewer bits per weight speeds things up even though the arithmetic has not changed. And when policy documents talk about "chips", memory bandwidth matters as much as the headline operation count.

Here is the bound, which is a one-line division.
ai.frontier.compute-hardware.the-chip-is.rigor:
For autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, the time per token is bounded below by the time to move the parameters:
$$t \;\ge\; \frac{N\,b}{B},$$
$N$ parameters, $b$ bytes each, $B$ the memory bandwidth. Take $N=7\times10^{10}$, $b=2$ (16-bit), $B=3\times10^{12}$ bytes/s:
$$t \ge \frac{1.4\times10^{11}}{3\times10^{12}} = 46.7\ \text{ms} \approx 21\ \text{tokens/s},$$
and no amount of arithmetic throughput improves it.

The roofline framing: **arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved. Decoding does about $2N$ FLOPs per token per sequence while moving $Nb$ bytes once for the whole batch, so
$$I \approx \frac{2N\cdot\text{batch}}{Nb} = \frac{2\,\text{batch}}{b}.$$
At batch 1 in 16-bit that is 1 FLOP per byte, against a machine balance point of several hundred — you are two orders of magnitude below the roof, squarely memory-bound. Raise the batch and $I$ rises proportionally until you finally hit the compute ceiling. That is the entire reason inference is sold in batches.

Training is the other regime: every token in the sequence contributes gradients while the weights are read once, so intensity is high and training really is compute-bound. The $6ND$ count is the right model there. For generation, it is not.

recall.question: Why does batching make inference so much cheaper per user?

options.text: Because the model runs fewer layers when the batch is larger
options.why: the computation per sequence is identical; only the scheduling changes.

options.text: The weights are read from memory once and reused across the whole batch
options.why: arithmetic intensity rises until the chip is compute-bound.

options.text: Because the sequences share a cache of each other's results
options.why: different users' sequences share nothing; what is shared is the weight traffic.

ai.frontier.labs.the-nonprofit-that-need.title: Why AI labs have such strange corporate structures
ai.frontier.labs.the-nonprofit-that-need.hook: A charity cannot raise a billion dollars for chips. A normal company cannot credibly promise to stop. Every lab is an attempt to be both.
ai.frontier.labs.the-nonprofit-that-need.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.frontier.labs.the-nonprofit-that-need.body:
Every frontier lab is a contraption bolted together out of two incompatible needs, and the contraptions are worth reading as evidence rather than as public relations.

OpenAI began as a non-profit in 2015 and in March 2019 announced a "capped-profit" arm: investors' returns are capped — the first round at 100 times the investment — with anything above the cap flowing to the non-profit. Anthropic incorporated in Delaware as a public benefit corporation and in September 2023 described a Long-Term Benefit Trust, five financially disinterested trustees holding the right to elect a growing share of the board, reaching a majority within four years. DeepMind's 2014 sale came with an ethics board.

These specific arrangements change, and you should assume the ones above have been amended since. What does not change is the force producing them, and that force is arithmetic rather than ideology.
ai.frontier.labs.the-nonprofit-that-need.rigor:
Model a lab's costs. A training run is a **fixed cost** $F$, paid in full before anyone knows whether the result is any good. Serving the trained model costs a **marginal** $c$ per query. Average cost over $N$ queries:
$$AC(N)=\frac{F}{N}+c.$$
With $F$ in the hundreds of millions and $c$ in fractions of a cent, $AC$ is dominated by the first term until $N$ reaches the billions.

Three consequences drop out, none of them about anyone's intentions.

1. **You need a mass product or a patron.** There is no viable middle: a lab serving a million queries pays roughly a thousand times more per query than one serving a billion.
2. **The industry concentrates.** $AC$ is strictly decreasing in $N$ — the textbook condition for natural monopoly, the same shape as a railway or a power grid.
3. **The capital comes first.** $F$ must be raised *before* the experiment, from people who want a claim on the upside. A charter that caps or redirects that claim is the only lever a founder has.

Note what the arithmetic does *not* say. Nothing here makes the frontier permanently closed: $F$ falls as algorithms improve, so this year's frontier run is next year's ordinary one.

recall.question: Why does the economics of training runs push towards a few large labs?

options.text: Because the research talent is scarce and clusters together
options.why: talent mobility matters, but it does not produce the cost structure.

options.text: Because the cost is mostly fixed and paid up front, so average cost falls with scale
options.why: the standard natural-monopoly shape.

options.text: Because model weights are protected by patents
options.why: weights are generally not patented; exclusivity comes from cost, not law.

ai.frontier.labs.where-the-labs-came-fro.title: Where the handful of frontier labs came from
ai.frontier.labs.where-the-labs-came-fro.hook: "Frontier lab" is not a compliment. It names the handful of organisations that can afford the largest training runs.
ai.frontier.labs.where-the-labs-came-fro.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Opened on a list of founding dates; moved the idea to the first line so the card leads with a claim rather than a roll call.

ai.frontier.labs.where-the-labs-came-fro.body:
None of them started rich. Each was a few people with a thesis, and each found out the same thing: testing the thesis costs more than a university department can spend.

DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, and sold to Google in January 2014 for a price reported between \$400 and \$650 million, with an AI ethics board written into the deal. OpenAI was announced in December 2015 as a non-profit with \$1 billion pledged, founded by a group including Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, John Schulman and Wojciech Zaremba. Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven people who had left OpenAI, among them Dario and Daniela Amodei. In April 2023 Google folded its Brain team and DeepMind into one organisation.

The shape repeats, and it often repeats as a split: Anthropic's seven founders came out of OpenAI.

Which is what the phrase actually means. "Frontier lab" is a statement about capital and access to chips, not about who has the best ideas. The ideas are mostly published.

recall.question: What does "frontier lab" pick out?

options.text: The labs producing the most influential research papers
options.why: influential work comes from universities and small groups too; publication is not the constraint.

options.text: The few organisations able to afford training runs at the largest scale
options.why: it is a claim about capital and compute access, not about ideas.

options.text: Labs working on artificial general intelligence rather than applications
options.why: stated missions vary and are not what the term tracks.

ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.open-weights-.title: Open weights is not open source, and the gap is enormous
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.open-weights-.hook: Weights are the output of the build, not the build. You can run the model and change it; you can never check how it was made.
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.open-weights-.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.open-weights-.body:
Publishing a model's weights sounds like publishing source code. It is closer to publishing a compiled binary.

Weights are what the training process *produced*. Release them and someone can run the model, fine-tune it, take it apart and study what it has learned. What they cannot do is rebuild it: no training data, no filtering rules, no training code, and no way to afford the compute even if they had all three. So nobody outside can check a claim about how the thing was made — what it was trained on, what was filtered out, whether the benchmark was in the training set.

The Open Source Initiative made the distinction official in October 2024. To qualify as open-source AI under its definition you need three things: information about the data detailed enough that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system, the complete training and inference code, and the parameters. Most "open" releases publish the third.

"Open weights" is the accurate name, and it is not an insult — it is most of what a researcher actually wants. It is just not reproducibility, and the difference has teeth.
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.open-weights-.rigor:
Write the artifacts as weights $\theta$, data $D$, code $C$, compute budget $F$.

With $\theta$ alone you get everything *downstream* of the trained function: inference, fine-tuning, distillation, interpretability, evaluation. Reproduction needs $(D,C,F)$; verifying a provenance or contamination claim needs $D$. So the asymmetry is sharp — **auditing how a model was made is impossible from $\theta$, while changing what it does is cheap from $\theta$.**

How cheap: Qi et al. (2023) removed the safety training from a deployed commercial model by fine-tuning on ten adversarial examples for under twenty cents of API credit. Alignment behaviour is a thin layer over the base model, and fine-tuning access is enough to peel it. With published weights, even the API gatekeeper is gone.

And release is irreversible. There is no recall for $\theta$: once it is on a torrent, every future decision has already been made. So a release is not a bet on the average use of a model, it is a bet on the worst use anyone will find for it over its entire life — which is a much harder quantity to be confident about.

recall.question: What can you not do with a model's published weights?

options.text: Fine-tune it for a new task
options.why: that is one of the main things weights are good for, and it is cheap.

options.text: Verify claims about how it was trained
options.why: reproduction and provenance checks need the data and the training code, which weights do not contain.

options.text: Inspect its internal activations
options.why: interpretability work runs directly on weights; it needs nothing else.

sources.title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
sources.author: Qi et al.

ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.would-you-pub.title: You run the lab. Do you publish the weights?
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.would-you-pub.hook: The release decision that actually gets made is not "is this dangerous?". Everything is dangerous. Here is the question that replaces it.
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.would-you-pub.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.frontier.open-vs-closed.would-you-pub.body:
Your lab has trained a model that is clearly better than anything public at one narrow thing: reading a large codebase and finding exploitable bugs.

Defenders would use it to fix software that has been quietly broken for a decade. Attackers would use it to find the same bugs faster than anyone can patch them. Publishing is irreversible — no recall, and whatever restriction you fine-tuned in can be fine-tuned out for the price of a coffee. Keeping it closed means the only people who can audit it for bias, or study how it works, are the ones on your payroll.

Before you decide: what is the question you would actually want answered? And why is "is this model dangerous?" the wrong one?

recall.question: What is the question that replaces "is it dangerous?"
recall.answer: **Marginal risk.** How much does *this* release change what a determined attacker could already achieve with public tools, already-released models and a few weeks of work? A capability that three other open models already have adds little; a genuinely novel one adds a lot. It converts an unanswerable question — everything is dangerous — into a comparative one you can investigate, and it makes the answer depend on the state of the world at the moment of release. That is why the same model can be reasonable to release this year and not last.

sources.title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
sources.author: Qi et al.

ai.frontier.policy.a-law-had-to-pick-a-n.title: Regulation had to pick a number, so it picked a big one
ai.frontier.policy.a-law-had-to-pick-a-n.hook: How do you legislate a technology you cannot define? You regulate the electricity bill instead.
ai.frontier.policy.a-law-had-to-pick-a-n.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.frontier.policy.a-law-had-to-pick-a-n.body:
Writing a law about "AI" runs into a definitional swamp immediately: a spam filter, a credit model and a chatbot are all the same technology on paper. The instrument that emerged instead sidesteps definitions entirely. Do not regulate the capability. Regulate anything whose training consumed more than a stated number of arithmetic operations.

The EU's AI Act — Regulation 2024/1689, in force from 1 August 2024 — presumes a general-purpose model carries systemic risk when its training used more than $10^{25}$ floating-point operations.

The appeal is real. Compute is countable, auditable, bought from a handful of suppliers, hard to conceal, and correlated with capability. Compared to everything else on offer, that is a miracle of tractability.

The problem is that the correlation moves under your feet, and it moves in one direction.
ai.frontier.policy.a-law-had-to-pick-a-n.rigor:
Write capability as a function of **effective compute** $C_{\text{eff}} = A(t)\cdot C$, where $C$ is the raw operation count and $A(t)$ is an algorithmic-efficiency multiplier rising over time. Ho et al. (2024), over 200 language-model evaluations from 2012–2023, estimate that the compute needed to reach a fixed performance level halves roughly every 8 months (95% interval 5 to 14 months).

A statute fixes $C^{\star}$. It therefore gates the capability level $A(t)\,C^{\star}$, which drifts upward on that same clock. After $k$ doublings of $A$, a model trained with only $C^{\star}/2^{k}$ operations matches what $C^{\star}$ bought when the law was drafted — and sits legally below the line. Thresholds **loosen** automatically. A fixed number in a statute is a snapshot of an exchange rate between compute and capability, and the rate is not fixed.

The fixes are all awkward: index the threshold, revise it periodically, or pair it with capability evaluations that reintroduce the definitional problem you were escaping.

The counter-argument survives anyway, and it is the honest one: of every input to the pipeline, $C$ is the only one that is physically countable, concentrated in few hands, and hard to hide. Expect the numbers to change and the *structure* — pick a measurable proxy, attach duties above it — to stay.

recall.question: What happens to a fixed compute threshold as algorithms improve?

options.text: It catches more models over time, since models keep getting bigger
options.why: some grow, but the threshold's meaning is about capability per unit of compute.

options.text: It gates a steadily higher capability level
options.why: so equally capable models slip below the line and escape it.

options.text: Nothing
options.why: it is a fixed physical quantity, so it stays constant in meaning — the quantity is fixed; what it buys in capability is not.

ai.frontier.policy.there-is-no-ai-regula.title: There is no AI regulator, and that is the point
ai.frontier.policy.there-is-no-ai-regula.hook: Most of what people want from AI regulation is already illegal. The interesting question is who enforces it.
ai.frontier.policy.there-is-no-ai-regula.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.frontier.policy.there-is-no-ai-regula.body:
People picture AI policy as one agency with one rulebook. Nowhere has that. Structurally there are four layers, and most of the weight sits on the first.

**Existing law already applies.** A discriminatory hiring model breaks employment law. A model that defames you is covered by defamation law. A diagnostic device is a medical device whether or not it contains a neural network. No new statute required, and this layer is doing most of the work right now.

**Sectoral regulators** interpret that law for their patch — medicines, finance, aviation — which is why the same model faces heavy duties in a hospital and none in a video game.

**Horizontal rules** cut across sectors: risk tiers, transparency duties, incident reporting, pre-deployment evaluation. The EU's AI Act is the main worked example.

**Supply-chain measures** act on the inputs rather than the model — export controls on chips, government procurement rules, cloud reporting requirements.

So when someone asks whether AI should be regulated, the useful reply is: which layer? They have different enforcers, different standards of evidence, and wildly different speeds.

recall.question: Which layer currently does most of the regulating of AI systems?

options.text: Dedicated AI statutes such as the EU's AI Act
options.why: important and growing, but recent, and narrower than the law that already exists.

options.text: Ordinary existing law
options.why: employment, consumer protection, medical devices, defamation — applied to systems that happen to contain a model.

options.text: Export controls on chips
options.why: powerful, but they act on who can build models, not on how deployed systems may behave.

ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.published-.title: The transformer was published as a translation result
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.published-.hook: No language model appears anywhere in the abstract. The headline result is a German translation score.
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.published-.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.published-.body: "Attention Is All You Need", posted 12 June 2017, is a machine-translation paper. Its headline numbers are BLEU scores: 28.4 on WMT 2014 English-to-German, 41.8 English-to-French, after 3.5 days on eight GPUs. The pitch is efficiency — same quality, far less training. Eight authors share a footnote reading "Equal contribution. Listing order is random." Nothing in the abstract mentions language modelling, chatbots or general capability.

recall.question: What was the 2017 transformer paper claiming?
recall.answer: A better speed/quality tradeoff on machine translation — 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German in 3.5 days on eight GPUs. Everything the architecture later became was downstream of a translation benchmark.

ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.won-by-del.title: The architecture that won by deleting something
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.won-by-del.hook: The most consequential architecture of the decade was defined by what its authors threw out.
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.won-by-del.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.won-by-del.body:
A recurrent network reads a sentence the way you do: one word, then the next, carrying a memory forward. That sounds like a virtue. It is a scheduling disaster. Word 500 cannot be computed until words 1 through 499 have been, one at a time, while a chip with thousands of arithmetic units stands in a queue.

The 2017 move was subtraction. Delete recurrence. Let every position look at every other position simultaneously, in one matrix operation, and let the model work out which of them matter.

Two things change at once. The sequence stops being a sequence as far as the hardware is concerned — the whole sentence is processed in parallel. And any two words become one step apart, however far apart they sit, so the signal connecting "the animal" to "it" forty words later no longer has to survive forty hops.

It bought all that with a cost, and the cost is what makes long context expensive. Here is the ledger.
ai.history.attention-2017-gpt.won-by-del.rigor:
From the paper's own comparison table, for sequence length $n$ and representation width $d$:

| layer | work per layer | sequential steps | max path length |
|---|---|---|---|
| self-attention | $O(n^2 d)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| recurrent | $O(n d^2)$ | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| convolutional, kernel $k$ | $O(k n d^2)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(\log_k n)$ |

Two columns are the argument. **Sequential steps** is what the GPU cannot parallelise: $O(1)$ versus $O(n)$. **Maximum path length** is the number of layers a gradient must travel between two positions; at $O(1)$, the vanishing-gradient problem over long ranges — the reason LSTM gates were invented — stops being an architectural problem and becomes an optimisation detail.

The price is the first column. Attention is quadratic in $n$ because every position attends to every position: doubling the context quadruples the work and the memory for the score matrix. In 2017, with sentences where $n < d$, self-attention was also *cheaper* per layer than recurrence. The moment contexts grew past a few thousand tokens, that $n^2$ became the central engineering problem of the field.

recall.question: What did removing recurrence buy?

options.text: Fewer parameters for the same quality
options.why: transformers are not generally smaller; the gain was in how the computation is scheduled.

options.text: A constant number of sequential steps and a constant path between any two positions
options.why: the sequence becomes parallel and long-range gradients stop decaying.

options.text: Linear rather than quadratic cost in sequence length
options.why: the opposite: attention costs $O(n^2)$, which is why context length is expensive.

ai.history.backprop-connectionism.invent.title: Backprop was invented at least three times before 1986
ai.history.backprop-connectionism.invent.hook: The algorithm behind every neural network was published in 1970, in Finnish, in a thesis about rounding errors.
ai.history.backprop-connectionism.invent.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.backprop-connectionism.invent.body:
Seppo Linnainmaa, master's thesis, University of Helsinki, 1970: *the representation of the cumulative rounding error of an algorithm as a Taylor expansion of the local rounding errors*. It contains the reverse mode of automatic differentiation — backpropagation, in full generality, on arbitrary sparsely connected computation graphs. It does not mention neural networks. He was worried about floating-point error.

Paul Werbos, Harvard PhD thesis, 1974, did apply it to neural networks, and spent years being told it was not interesting. Go back further and the continuous-time version is standard optimal control: Kelley in 1960, Bryson in 1961, Pontryagin's adjoint method underneath both.

Then on 9 October 1986, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published "Learning representations by back-propagating errors" in *Nature*, and the field woke up.

Read their title again. The claim is not the algorithm — it is *representations*. What they showed was that the hidden units, trained this way, invent useful features nobody specified. An algorithm becomes an invention on the day somebody shows what it is for.

recall.question: What did the 1986 Nature paper contribute?

options.text: The backpropagation algorithm itself
options.why: reverse-mode differentiation was published by Linnainmaa in 1970 and applied to nets by Werbos in 1974.

options.text: The demonstration that hidden layers trained this way learn useful internal representations
options.why: that is what made the old algorithm matter.

options.text: A proof that gradient descent finds the global optimum
options.why: no such proof exists; deep networks are famously non-convex.

ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.thirty-eig.title: The program that proved 38 theorems and got rejected anyway
ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.thirty-eig.hook: It found a proof shorter than Whitehead and Russell's, and a journal declined the paper because one author was a program.
ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.thirty-eig.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.thirty-eig.body:
Everyone at Dartmouth in 1956 arrived with a plan. Allen Newell, Herbert Simon and Cliff Shaw arrived with something running.

Logic Theorist worked through the propositional logic of Whitehead and Russell's *Principia Mathematica* and proved 38 of the first 52 theorems of Chapter 2. For theorem 2.85 it found a proof shorter than the one in the book. Simon wrote to Russell about it; Russell wrote back delighted. Then, as Simon told the story, they sent a paper to the *Journal of Symbolic Logic* listing Logic Theorist as a co-author, and it was declined.

The method matters more than the score. Logic Theorist did not enumerate derivations — that space is far too big. It worked backwards from the goal and used rough rules to decide which branch looked promising. Search plus heuristics. For the next twenty years, that was what "artificial intelligence" meant.

recall.question: What was the key idea in Logic Theorist?

options.text: Enumerating every possible proof until one works
options.why: the space of derivations is astronomically large; brute force was exactly what it avoided.

options.text: Searching backwards from the goal with heuristics ranking which branch to try
options.why: search guided by rules of thumb became the template for symbolic AI.

options.text: Learning proof strategies from a corpus of existing proofs
options.why: learning from data came much later; its knowledge was hand-written.

ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.two-months.title: Two months, ten men, and the word that stuck
ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.two-months.hook: The field of artificial intelligence got its name inside a grant application, and the budget was two months.
ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.two-months.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.dartmouth-symbolic.two-months.body:
A whole research field is named in one sentence of a funding request. Dated 31 August 1955, signed by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon:

> We propose that a 2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence be carried out during the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire.

The working hypothesis is the next line: that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be described so precisely that a machine can simulate it.

McCarthy later wrote that he coined "artificial intelligence" partly to get out from under "cybernetics" — which would have meant accepting Norbert Wiener as the field's guru, or else arguing with him.

The workshop itself was a mess. People arrived and left on their own schedules, nobody agreed on an agenda, and the summer produced no shared theory. What it did produce was a name, a mailing list, and the conviction that this was one subject rather than six. Those turn out to be the hard parts.

recall.question: What did the Dartmouth proposal actually commit to?

options.text: Building a working thinking machine within two months
options.why: it set a research agenda; nobody promised a finished machine.

options.text: A two-month study resting on the conjecture that intelligence can be described precisely enough to simulate
options.why: that conjecture is the field's founding bet.

options.text: Proving that machines cannot think without a body
options.why: embodiment critiques came decades later, from other people.

sources.title: A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester & Shannon

ai.history.deep-learning-2012.the-unfash.title: The unfashionable idea that made deep learning work
ai.history.deep-learning-2012.the-unfash.hook: The paper that cracked computer vision was a poster. What made it possible was years of paying strangers to label photographs.
ai.history.deep-learning-2012.the-unfash.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.deep-learning-2012.the-unfash.body:
In 2006 the fashionable move in computer vision was a cleverer algorithm on a few thousand images. Fei-Fei Li bet the other way: the models were not starving for cleverness, they were starving for examples.

So ImageNet was not research, it was logistics. Categories borrowed from WordNet's hierarchy of English nouns. Labelling farmed out on Amazon Mechanical Turk: 49,000 workers across 167 countries, filtering and labelling over 160 million candidate images between July 2008 and April 2010, each surviving image checked by several people. The result was more than 14 million labelled photographs across 20,000-plus categories.

The 2009 paper announcing it was a poster at CVPR. The competition that ran on a 1,000-category slice — about 1.28 million training images — started in 2010 and was won twice by hand-designed features before a neural network turned up in 2012.

Datasets are infrastructure. Infrastructure is invisible until the thing it carries arrives.

recall.question: What was Fei-Fei Li's bet in starting ImageNet?

options.text: That better architectures would emerge if researchers had a standard benchmark
options.why: standardised evaluation helped, but the bet was about scale.

options.text: That the limiting factor was the number of labelled examples, not the sophistication of the algorithm
options.why: so she spent years on data instead of models.

options.text: That hand-designed features would beat learned ones given enough images
options.why: the opposite; learned features won the moment the data was big enough.

sources.title: ImageNet: A large-scale hierarchical image database
sources.author: Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li & Fei-Fei

ai.history.deep-learning-2012.two-gaming.title: Two gaming cards, six days, and vision fell over
ai.history.deep-learning-2012.two-gaming.hook: Eleven percentage points is not an improvement. It is a change of era, and it arrived on two consumer graphics cards.
ai.history.deep-learning-2012.two-gaming.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Swapped the NeurIPS abstract page for the PDF: only the PDF carries the 15.3%/26.2% sentence. Hook and body now agree on the 10.9-point gap.

ai.history.deep-learning-2012.two-gaming.body:
The ImageNet competition results went up on 30 September 2012. AlexNet's top-5 error: 15.3%. The runner-up, built on decades of carefully hand-designed image features: 26.2%.

Competitions are usually won by a fraction of a point. Almost eleven means the second-place method was not a rival, it was a previous era.

The hardware is the part people forget. Alex Krizhevsky trained 60 million parameters on two NVIDIA GTX 580 cards — gaming hardware, 3 GB of memory each — for five to six days, ninety passes over 1.2 million photographs. No supercomputer, no cluster.

Nothing in the design was new in principle. Convolution came from LeCun in the late 1980s, the training algorithm from 1986 or 1970 depending on who you credit. What was new was that all of it ran at once, on a dataset large enough to reward it. Within two years essentially every serious entry in the competition was a deep network.

recall.question: What was actually new about AlexNet?
recall.answer: Almost none of the ingredients. Convolution, backpropagation and the GPU all predate it. What was new was the combination running at scale on a dataset of over a million labelled images.

sources.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
sources.author: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton

ai.history.games-milestones.la-maquina-q.title: La máquina que ganó y a la que nunca le pidieron revancha
ai.history.games-milestones.la-maquina-q.hook: Deep Blue ganó sin aprender nada. Buscaba 200 millones de posiciones por segundo y evaluaba con reglas escritas a mano.
ai.history.games-milestones.la-maquina-q.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.games-milestones.la-maquina-q.body:
Nueva York, 11 de mayo de 1997. Deep Blue le gana a Gari Kaspárov 3½ a 2½. Un año antes, en Filadelfia, Kaspárov había ganado 4 a 2; en doce meses IBM duplicó la velocidad de la máquina.

Los números: 480 chips de ajedrez diseñados a medida, 30 procesadores, 200 millones de posiciones por segundo. Y ni un gramo de aprendizaje. Deep Blue buscaba a lo bruto y evaluaba cada posición con una función que escribieron humanos, ajustada a mano con ayuda de grandes maestros. No mejoraba jugando. Apagada y encendida, era exactamente la misma.

Lo más bonito es lo que pasó en la cabeza de Kaspárov. Se ha reportado que la jugada 44 de la primera partida salió de un mecanismo de emergencia que dispara cuando la máquina no logra decidir. Kaspárov la leyó como una profundidad que no entendía, y esa sospecha lo acompañó el resto del duelo. Acusó a IBM de intervención humana. IBM retiró la máquina y le negó la revancha: un rack quedó en un museo de Washington y el otro en el Computer History Museum.

recall.question: ¿Por qué Deep Blue no cuenta como un sistema que aprende?
recall.answer: Porque su conocimiento estaba escrito por humanos: una función de evaluación ajustada a mano y una búsqueda enorme. Jugar partidas no cambiaba nada dentro de la máquina.

ai.history.games-milestones.why-go-held-.title: Remember why Go was supposed to be safe from computers?
ai.history.games-milestones.why-go-held-.hook: Chess fell in 1997. Go held out until 2016. The gap is not nineteen years of hardware — it is one missing function.
ai.history.games-milestones.why-go-held-.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.games-milestones.why-go-held-.body:
A chess board has 64 squares and a Go board has 361, and that is the usual explanation for why Deep Blue won in 1997 while Go survived another nineteen years. Board size is real, but it is not the reason.

Deep Blue's method has two halves. Look ahead through possible moves; then, where you stop looking, *score* the position you reached and back the best score up. Go breaks both halves, but only one fatally.

The first half is arithmetic. Chess offers about 35 legal moves per turn, Go about 250, so each extra layer of lookahead costs seven times more. Painful, survivable, and hardware eats into it yearly.

The second half is the wall. In chess you can score a position by counting material — a queen is worth nine pawns, and that crude sum is startlingly good. In Go every stone is identical and worth nothing alone; a position's value lives in shape and influence. Nobody could write that function, and forty years of people tried.

Go did not need faster search. It needed a machine that could *learn what a position is worth*.
ai.history.games-milestones.why-go-held-.rigor:
Game-tree size is roughly $b^d$ for branching factor $b$ and depth $d$. Chess: $b\approx 35$, $d\approx 80$, giving Shannon's 1950 estimate of about $10^{120}$. Go: $b\approx 250$, $d\approx 150$, about $10^{360}$. Tromp counted the legal 19×19 positions exactly in 2016: $2.08\times 10^{170}$.

Both are unsearchable, so the exponent is not what separates them. What separates them is what alpha–beta pruning needs. With perfect move ordering, alpha–beta visits about $b^{d/2}$ nodes — it turns $35^{80}$ into $35^{40}$, a genuine miracle and still astronomical. Chess programs survive by cutting the search off at depth 12–20 and calling a **static evaluation function** on the leaves. The whole scheme rests on that function existing and being cheap.

So the binding constraint is not $b$, it is the leaf evaluator. AlphaGo supplied one by learning it: a value network $v_\theta(s)$ estimating the probability of winning from position $s$, trained on self-play, plus a policy network to order moves. The exponent stayed enormous; the search simply stopped needing to reach the end.

recall.question: Why did Go resist computer play so much longer than chess?

options.text: Its game tree is too large to search
options.why: both trees are hopelessly large; chess programs never searched theirs either.

options.text: No cheap hand-written way to score a position existed
options.why: and search with a depth cutoff depends entirely on having one.

options.text: Go has no equivalent of alpha–beta pruning
options.why: alpha–beta applies to any two-player zero-sum game, Go included.

sources.title: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search
sources.author: Silver et al.

ai.history.perceptron-feud.conscious-of-.title: The Navy announced a machine that would be conscious of its existence
ai.history.perceptron-feud.conscious-of-.hook: In 1958 the US Navy told reporters it had the embryo of a computer that would one day be conscious of its existence.
ai.history.perceptron-feud.conscious-of-.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: The convergence theorem was proved in 1962 (Rosenblatt's book, Novikoff independently), not before the 1958 press release. Dated it.

ai.history.perceptron-feud.conscious-of-.body:
The first AI hype cycle ran in 1958, and the *New York Times* did the honours. The Navy, it reported, had revealed the embryo of an electronic computer that it expected would "be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence."

The actual machine, Frank Rosenblatt's Mark I Perceptron, was a room of hardware wired to 400 cadmium-sulfide photocells in a 20×20 grid. Its adjustable weights were potentiometers, physically turned by little electric motors as it learned. It could be trained to tell simple shapes apart. That is all it could do.

But underneath the press release sat a genuine theorem, proved in Rosenblatt's 1962 book and independently by Novikoff the same year: if the categories can be separated by a straight cut through the input space, his learning rule finds such a cut, in a finite number of corrections, from any starting point. A machine that provably learns. No wonder people lost their heads.

The trouble was the word *if*.

recall.question: What did Rosenblatt's convergence theorem actually promise?
recall.answer: That if the two classes are linearly separable, the perceptron learning rule reaches a separating boundary after finitely many mistakes. It promises nothing at all when they are not.

sources.title: The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain
sources.author: Frank Rosenblatt

ai.history.perceptron-feud.the-book-that.title: The book everyone blames for the first neural-network winter
ai.history.perceptron-feud.the-book-that.hook: They were classmates at the same high school. One wrote the book that is blamed for burying the other's life's work.
ai.history.perceptron-feud.the-book-that.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: The 'sterile' verdict is the 1969 book's own conjecture, not a fresh 1988 judgement; rewrote that sentence. The 1988 edition reprinted the text with a new prologue and epilogue, no retraction.

ai.history.perceptron-feud.the-book-that.body:
Marvin Minsky and Frank Rosenblatt were at the Bronx High School of Science together, a year apart. They spent the 1960s arguing in public about whether learning machines were a serious idea. In 1969 Minsky and Seymour Papert published *Perceptrons*. In July 1971, on his 43rd birthday, Rosenblatt drowned in a boating accident on Chesapeake Bay.

The standard story — the book killed the field for fifteen years — is a legend. Funding for connectionism did collapse, but military money was already rotating away from it, and the work never stopped: Amari, Grossberg, Fukushima and Werbos all published through the supposed dead years.

What is documented is the reception. Jordan Pollack's verdict is that a narrow proof about a global issue was read as a successful attempt to bury the whole idea. The famous word is theirs, and it is from 1969, not from the backprop era: they called the extension to many-layered machines *sterile* and invited the field to reject that judgement. Nobody did for seventeen years, and the 1988 expanded edition reprinted the text with a fresh prologue and epilogue — no retraction.

recall.question: How should you treat "Minsky's book caused the first AI winter"?

options.text: As established fact
options.why: funding fell right afterwards, which settles it — correlation with a funding shift that was already under way is not causation.

options.text: As a contested claim
options.why: the funding collapse had several causes and connectionist research continued through the 1970s.

options.text: As pure myth with nothing behind it
options.why: the book was genuinely influential on how the field read the evidence; the dispute is about how much.

ai.history.perceptron-feud.what-minsky-a.title: What Minsky and Papert actually proved
ai.history.perceptron-feud.what-minsky-a.hook: Everyone says the 1969 book proved a perceptron can't do XOR. XOR was the easy part and everyone already knew it.
ai.history.perceptron-feud.what-minsky-a.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Added a related link to the neural-nets XOR card, which shares the impossibility proof.

ai.history.perceptron-feud.what-minsky-a.body:
The legend is that in 1969 two MIT professors proved a perceptron cannot compute XOR, and neural networks died of embarrassment. XOR is four points and a two-line contradiction; nobody needed a book for it, and Minsky and Papert knew perfectly well that stacking layers fixes it.

The book's real subject is *how much each feature detector has to see*. Give a perceptron any collection of little detectors, each looking at a handful of pixels, and add up their votes. The question is how big a handful you need. Their answer: for some perfectly ordinary visual predicates, you need detectors that see essentially the whole image. Parity — is the number of lit pixels odd? — requires one detector covering every pixel. Connectedness — is this shape one piece or two? — cannot be settled by detectors with bounded receptive fields at all.

That is an argument about locality and scale, and it applies to any architecture built from local parts. Their actual charge against multilayer networks was different and, in 1969, true: nobody had a learning theorem for them.
ai.history.perceptron-feud.what-minsky-a.rigor:
A perceptron computes $\psi(X) = \big[\sum_i w_i\,\varphi_i(X) > \theta\big]$, where each $\varphi_i$ is a predicate on a subset $S_i$ of the retina. The **order** of $\psi$ is the smallest $k$ with $|S_i| \le k$ for all $i$.

*XOR has order 2.* Suppose a single linear unit computed it: $w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 > \theta$ exactly on $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$. Then $0 \le \theta$, $w_1 > \theta$, $w_2 > \theta$, and $w_1 + w_2 \le \theta$. Adding the middle two gives $w_1 + w_2 > 2\theta \ge \theta$ — a contradiction. That is the whole "XOR problem": the picture on this card is the proof.

*Parity has order $n$.* By their Group Invariance Theorem, a predicate invariant under all permutations of the retina admits a solution whose weights depend only on $|S_i|$, so $\psi$ reduces to the sign of a polynomial $p(|X|)$ of degree $\le k$. Parity must change sign at each of $|X| = 0,1,\dots,n$, forcing $n$ roots, so $k \ge n$. One detector must watch every pixel.

The order is the bound on the *handful* from the intuition — and order $n$ means there is no local shortcut, whatever the hardware.

recall.question: What does "a predicate of order $n$" mean for a perceptron with $n$ inputs?

options.text: It needs $n$ layers to compute
options.why: order counts how many inputs a single detector reads, not how deep the network is.

options.text: Some feature detector must look at all $n$ inputs at once
options.why: no assembly of locally-limited detectors can compute it, however many you use.

options.text: It needs at least $n$ training examples
options.why: order is a property of the function, not of the data you fit it on.

ai.history.turing-cybernetics.imitation-.title: The Turing test began as a game about telling men from women
ai.history.turing-cybernetics.imitation-.hook: Before a machine was allowed into it, Turing's test was a parlour game about telling a man from a woman.
ai.history.turing-cybernetics.imitation-.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.turing-cybernetics.imitation-.body:
Turing's 1950 paper opens with a game that has no machine in it. Three people: a man (A), a woman (B), and an interrogator (C) who sees neither and communicates by note. C must work out which is which. A's job is to deceive; B's is to help. Turing even supplies a sample question: "Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?"

Only then comes the swerve. "What will happen when a machine takes the part of A in this game?"

So the original test is not "can a machine pass for a human". It is: can a machine deceive as well as a man pretending to be a woman? Imitation under an assumed identity was in the design from the first paragraph.

He also set a deadline. In about fifty years, he wrote, a computer with storage of about $10^9$ would play well enough that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 per cent chance of identifying correctly after five minutes. Read that again: he predicted a machine that fools you three times in ten. Not a pass. A respectable failure.

recall.question: In Turing's original setup, what is the machine replacing?
recall.answer: Player A — the man who is trying to convince the interrogator that he is the woman. The test was built on imitation under a false identity, not on "acting human" in general.

ai.history.turing-cybernetics.too-meanin.title: Turing thought his own question was meaningless
ai.history.turing-cybernetics.too-meanin.hook: Turing opened the founding paper of AI with a question, then threw the question away.
ai.history.turing-cybernetics.too-meanin.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.turing-cybernetics.too-meanin.body:
He opens with "I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'" Six sections later, in *Mind*, October 1950:

> The original question, "Can machines think?" I believe to be too meaningless to deserve discussion.

His reason is not modesty. "Machine" and "think" cannot be defined without smuggling the answer in, so he replaced the question with a game that has a score. Seventy-odd years of arguing about whether a program *really* understands is an argument about the exact thing Turing refused to have.

ai.history.winters-expert-systems.lighth.title: One report, and British AI lost its funding
ai.history.winters-expert-systems.lighth.hook: A fluid dynamicist was asked to review AI in 1973. British AI research did not recover for a decade.
ai.history.winters-expert-systems.lighth.author: author-ai-history-1

reviewed.notes: Cut the unsupported 'they lost' about the 1973 BBC debate; the verifiable outcome is the funding withdrawal, which is what the sentence now carries.

ai.history.winters-expert-systems.lighth.body:
The Science Research Council wanted an outsider's opinion, so it asked Sir James Lighthill — an eminent fluid dynamicist with no stake in the field. His 1973 survey, *Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey*, divided the subject into three: A for advanced automation, C for computer-based studies of the nervous system, and B for the "bridge" between them, the robotics work that was supposed to connect the two. His verdict on all of it:

> In no part of the field have the discoveries made so far produced the major impact that was then promised.

Category B, he argued, had no results of its own and survived by borrowing justification from A and C. The technical charge was the combinatorial explosion: methods that shine on toy problems grow exponentially with the size of the problem, so success on a blocks-world demo predicts nothing about the real one.

On 9 May 1973 the BBC televised a debate at the Royal Institution — Lighthill against Donald Michie, John McCarthy and Richard Gregory. Whoever won the evening lost the argument that counted: the report became the basis for withdrawing government support from AI at most British universities.

recall.question: What was Lighthill's central technical objection?
recall.answer: The combinatorial explosion: search-based methods scale exponentially with problem size, so a program that solves a toy version tells you nothing about the real one. Demos were not evidence.

ai.history.winters-expert-systems.the-bo.title: The second AI boom died of maintenance
ai.history.winters-expert-systems.the-bo.hook: An expert system saved one company an estimated 25 million dollars a year. Five years later the whole industry was gone.
ai.history.winters-expert-systems.the-bo.author: author-ai-history-1
ai.history.winters-expert-systems.the-bo.body:
Expert systems were the comeback. Instead of general intelligence, bottle one specialist's knowledge as if-then rules and run it. It genuinely worked. MYCIN diagnosed bacterial infections about as well as Stanford faculty. XCON, written by John McDermott at Carnegie Mellon in 1978 and running at Digital Equipment from 1980, configured VAX orders: roughly 2,500 rules, 80,000 orders processed, and an estimated saving of \$25 million a year by 1986.

Then it collapsed. The specialised Lisp hardware market died in 1987, Japan's decade-long Fifth Generation project ended without its goals, and "expert system" became a word you did not put in a grant application.

The cause was not intelligence. It was upkeep. Every awkward new case needs a new rule, someone has to sit with an expert to extract it, and each rule can interact with every rule already there. The knowledge base grows linearly and the cost of owning it does not.
ai.history.winters-expert-systems.the-bo.rigor:
Two scaling arguments, neither fixed by a faster machine.

**Search.** Chaining rules to depth $d$ with branching factor $b$ explores $O(b^d)$ states. With $b=10$ and $d=10$ that is $10^{10}$ — Lighthill's combinatorial explosion. Pruning it requires knowing which branches are hopeless, which is more knowledge, which is more rules.

**Maintenance.** A base of $n$ rules has $\binom{n}{2} = \Theta(n^2)$ potential pairwise interactions: contradictions, shadowing, ordering effects. If validating a new rule means checking it against what is already there, adding rule $n+1$ costs $\Theta(n)$ and building the base from scratch costs
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} \Theta(k) = \Theta(n^2).$$
Doubling the knowledge quadruples the work of keeping it consistent.

Both are the same complaint the intuition made: the upkeep, not the reasoning. And both point at the same exit. You cannot out-write $n^2$ by hiring more knowledge engineers; you have to get the rules from data instead of from people. That exit is machine learning, and it took another twenty-five years to become affordable.

recall.question: Why did expert systems stall even though individual systems worked?

options.text: The inference engines were too slow for real problems
options.why: hardware speed was not the binding constraint; rule bases were small by modern standards.

options.text: The cost of writing and reconciling rules grew faster than the knowledge did
options.why: roughly $n^2$ interactions for $n$ rules, all of it hand-checked.

options.text: They were provably unable to represent expert knowledge
options.why: rule bases did capture real expertise; MYCIN matched faculty diagnosticians.

ai.interpretability.circuits.the-head-th.title: The two-head circuit that finishes a pattern you just showed it
ai.interpretability.circuits.the-head-th.hook: Look back for the last time this token appeared, take whatever came next, predict that. A whole mechanism, located and verified.
ai.interpretability.circuits.the-head-th.author: author-ai-theory-1
ai.interpretability.circuits.the-head-th.body:
Give a language model an invented name, use it once, then start it again — "Mr Dursleth … Mr Durs" — and it will finish the word. Nothing in its training data covers your particular invention. It is copying a pattern from earlier in the same context, and that ability is most of what people mean by in-context learning.

Olsson and colleagues located the mechanism in 2022 and named it the induction head. It is a circuit made of two attention heads in different layers. The first, at every position, writes into the residual stream a record of what the *previous* token was. The second searches back for a position whose record matches the current token, and copies forward whatever followed it. The rule it implements is literally [A][B] … [A] → [B].

Two things lift this above storytelling. It is testable by ablation: delete those heads and the copying goes. And it *forms* at a sharp phase change during training — a visible bump in the loss curve — at the same moment in-context learning appears.
ai.interpretability.circuits.the-head-th.rigor:
In a transformer, head $h$ at position $i$ computes $\sum_j\alpha^{h}_{ij}\,W^{h}_{OV}x_j$ with $\alpha^{h}_{ij}\propto\exp\!\big(x_i^{\top}W^{h}_{QK}x_j\big)$, where $W_{QK}=W_Q^{\top}W_K$ and $W_{OV}=W_OW_V$ are the two bilinear forms that characterise a head (Elhage et al., 2021).

The induction circuit is a **K-composition** of two heads. A previous-token head in an early layer copies $x_{j-1}$ into the residual stream at position $j$. The induction head in a later layer then reads that as its key, so its query–key score at $(i,j)$ is effectively $x_i^{\top}W_{QK}\,x_{j-1}$ — it attends to positions whose *predecessor* matches the current token. Its $W_{OV}$ is approximately a copy map, so what comes out is $x_j$: the token that followed last time.

The evidence Olsson et al. assemble is causal, not narrative. Ablating the identified heads degrades in-context learning; the improvement in loss attributable to long context appears exactly when induction heads form; and the same heads generalise to literal copying, pattern completion and rough translation.

The honest limit: clean, verified circuits like this come from small attention-only models. At production scale the same analysis is far harder — which is the gap sparse dictionary methods were built to close.

recall.question: What does an induction head do?

options.text: It finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies whatever followed it
options.why: the pattern [A][B] … [A] → [B].

options.text: It memorises frequent bigrams from the training data
options.why: the striking part is that it works on sequences never seen in training, using context alone.

options.text: It attends to the most semantically similar earlier token
options.why: the match is on the *previous-token* record, which is exactly what makes it a two-head composition.
